results.title: The AI cloud math is broken, and it’s creating a power shift within Big Tech - MarketWatch
highlights:
## Buying AI hardware outright is becoming more economical than renting AI power through the cloud

By 

Jurica Dujmovic

Sept. 3, 2026, 7:00 a.m. ET

Renting computing power has stopped getting cheaper fast enough to matter.

In July, I spent €64,780, or about $75,500, on four artificial-intelligence graphics cards and the server that holds them, rather than renting the same processing power from Amazon.com AMZN by the hour. And if enough companies run that calculation at a much greater scale, it changes who profits from the AI boom.

Let’s look at the math: When it went on sale in April 2025, the Nvidia NVDA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell was initially listed at $8,565. By June 2026, the price jumped up to $13,250. In August 2026, those who wanted the graphics card needed to shell out a staggering $16,000, or roughly 87% above the initial price.

results.title: Investing in Neoclouds Part 2  - by Blake Callahan
highlights:
Applied Digital owns two layers and rents them out. IREN owns all six. Nebius owns most of them. ... That map explains most of the financial results below.

...

Nebius grew 454% year over year.

...

IREN is the only company with declining revenue, which is from this long bitcoin to AI compute transition. Revenue fell $7.6 million sequentially as bitcoin miners were swapped out for AI GPUs. AI cloud revenue doubled during the quarter to $70.5 million. Meanwhile, mining revenue fell to $66.7 million and $638.8 million of hardware was written off. Adjusted EBITDA has fallen for five straight quarters, from $121.9 million down to $19.2 million. The next big event is Horizons 2 - 4 landing in Q4 2026, with revenue arriving mostly in the March 2027 quarter. 

Applied Digital reported revenue up 407% to $258.7 million in its May quarter, but $152.4 million of the $203.0 million HPC line was one-time tenant fit-out billed at construction margins. Recurring base rent was $44.1 million and full-year NOI was $90.4 million. 

Compared to where they are today, these compute sales targets are all ambitious. CoreWeave is at roughly $10.3 billion on Q2 revenue annualized, so it needs to essentially double. Nebius is at $3.0 billion and needs to nearly triple. IREN is at $1.0 billion and needs to quadruple. Applied Digital publishes no run rate, only NOI, which is why it is not on the chart. How they can do it is by the rising price of AI compute. 

Nebius currently bills between $9 million and $14 million dollars, with $12 million average. They are signing new deals at over $20 million dollars per megawatt. Q2 deals closed at $20 to $25 million, and the first short-term deal, signed in early Q3, priced above $40 million. Compute prices are rising rapidly, while also delivering new capacity quickly. Nebius raised prices on older-generation GPUs by more than 30% over Q1. Most of the step from $12 million to $20 million is longer term

IREN recent three-year contracts are priced above $20 million per megawatt with active discussions near $25 million, but the contracted book sits well below that. Microsoft is $9.7 billion over five years against 200 MW of critical IT load, or $9.7 million per megawatt per year, and the $1 billion of ARR operating today runs near $10 million.

CoreWeave does not disclose its new contract values to investors. However, they did disclose that they raised prices 25% across teh board in July. And they are compleylty sold out. So we can understand that gimilir to NBIS, their older GPUs are sold out and prices have gone up. Overall, we can calculate a backlog of $104 billion against 3.7 GW of contracted power works out to $28 million per megawatt of total contract value. Roughly in line with what NBIS signed in the quarter. 

Applied Digital is a landlord, renting out space for a fixed rate of about 1.7 million dollars per megawatt. Because they use long-term leases, they collect exactly what they sign for. Their lower price reflects the fact that they provide the building, not the computers.

Layers = Millions = Value

The difference between earning $40 million per megawatt and $1.7 million is a function of how many layers a company owns. Applied Digital sells two layers while Nebius sells six. The value can be seen clearly to exist in these upper Neocloud layers. For that reason, I’m going to drop Applied Digital from our conversation. Too much debt, too little to gain from an all consuming AI compute future. So let’s look to value the three remaining companies.

...

Both of their short-term cash and receivables is very close to their total debt. They’re both around 7- 8 billion. 

CRWV has $51.4 billion across debt and leases, against $7 billion of cash with total liabilities over $72 billion. If compute prices stall or change direction or new GPUs come out and lower the price per token, basically if anything happens this company just so over leveraged that I have to eliminate it here.

highlights:
# [SMM Computing Power News] H100 rental budgets left behind, current quotes 6%–15% higher than July

Published: Sep 03, 2026 16:18 (GMT+8)

SMM learned that on July 20, a lessee with demand for renting eight H100 full servers set a budget of 71,000 yuan per unit per month. Against the current market, mainstream quotations for this model have risen to 75,000–82,000 yuan per unit per month, with the lower end of the range exceeding the budget by 4,000 yuan and the upper end by 11,000 yuan, representing increases of 5.6%–15.5%. During this period, bulk resources in north China were quoted at 75,000 yuan for a four-year closed contract and 76,000 yuan for a five-year closed contract, while annual contracts in east China reached 82,000 yuan. SMM believes that the lessee's budget has been clearly outpaced by market prices within a month and a half, and the window for low-priced H100 resources has essentially closed.

# [SMM Computing Power Flash] Pro 6000 demand cools; 32 new machines in east China not yet listed, awaiting customers

Published: Sep 03, 2026 17:35 (GMT+8)

SMM has learned that a capital provider in east China has completed the construction and installation of 32 Pro 6000 eight-GPU full servers, but the units have not yet been put on racks, and no leasing clients have been secured. SMM previously collected a monthly rental quote of 36,000–37,000 yuan per unit per month for the Pro 6000. Recently, signs have also emerged of idle order circulation, with 32 units of the same scale being offered for lease while demand is simultaneously listed. Upstream delivery default risk is rising at the same time. SMM believes that this model uses GDDR7 memory rather than HBM, making it less suitable for training scenarios and leaving its positioning unclear. Coupled with leading cloud vendors bringing similar resources online in batches in September, later-stage demand and capacity face the risk of being squeezed.

results.title: The GPU Provider Shakeout: What Q1-Q2 Exits Taught | GPUaaS.com
highlights:
H100 spot fell to $1.99 an hour, below the cost basis for debt-financed providers. Five to seven are projected to survive from over a hundred. The mechanism, and what it means for buyers.

# The Provider Shakeout: What Q1-Q2 Exits Taught the Market

GPUaaS.com Team GPU Infrastructure September 3, 2026

H100 spot pricing fell to $1.99 an hour during the first half of 2026. That is below the cost basis for providers carrying debt-financed hardware.

Analysis across multiple sources now puts the number of GPU cloud providers likely to survive the next 18 to 24 months as standalone businesses at five to seven. There are well over a hundred competing today.

Key takeaways

- H100 spot fell to $1.99/hr, below the cost basis for debt-financed providers. Five to seven providers are projected to survive the next 18 to 24 months as standalone businesses
- A debt-financed cluster breaks even around 70 to 75% utilization. At 70%, right at the threshold, a 1,024-GPU H100 cluster still loses $80K to $130K a month
- Provider stress is visible before any announcement: capacity rationing, slower response for non-enterprise customers, sudden pricing changes
- Vendor-financed providers must price to cover both debt service and the vendor's revenue cut, so an unexplained premium may be structural rather than opportunistic
- Renewals from 2024-2025 land through late 2026 against a changed standard: sovereignty, geographic resilience, compliance, not just access

...

◆ A 1,024-GPU H100 CLUSTER, BY UTILIZATION

| Utilization | Monthly result |
| --- | --- |
| 55% | Loss of roughly $330,000 |
| 70% (near breakeven) | Loss of $80,000 to $130,000 |
| 85% | Gain of roughly $340,000 |
| 90% | Gain of $170,000 to $220,000 |

Sources: American Compute 2026 via ModulEdge for the 55% and 85% figures, Spheron cost model dated 4 July 2026 for the 70% and 90% figures. The two models use different rate and colocation assumptions, which is why the bands differ

...

A debt-financed cluster breaks even somewhere around 70 to 75% utilization. On a 1,024-GPU H100 cluster, 55% utilization produces a loss of roughly $330,000 a month while 85% produces a gain of roughly $340,000. Sit at 70%, right at the threshold, and the same cluster still loses $80,000 to $130,000 a month. Push to 90% and it generates $170,000 to $220,000. Bare-metal gross margins run 55 to 65% before depreciation is counted at all.

That is a business where a fifteen-point utilization swing decides solvency. When spot pricing falls below cost basis, the revenue side of that equation stops working regardless of how well the cluster is run.

...

Capital raised in a different interest rate environment came due. Debt service on hardware depreciating faster than model generations is brutal arithmetic, and it does not improve with time. Over a hundred providers were competing for investment precisely when investor scrutiny of unit economics intensified, which meant the capital needed to refresh aging fleets became hardest to raise at the moment it was most needed.

Chip availability shifted the advantage. Blackwell production ramping through 2026 expanded supply, which sounds helpful and was not, for smaller players. Expanded availability makes volume purchasing power and supplier relationships more decisive, not less. A provider without scale loses the pricing advantage that scarcity had been providing.

Hyperscaler price cuts closed the gap that justified the category. Neoclouds existed partly because they were cheaper than AWS and Azure. When the hyperscalers cut, the differentiation narrowed for providers who had nothing else to offer.

...

A capital-heavy provider under pressure has to keep utilization above a hard threshold or lose money every month. That constraint is real regardless of how the market eventually shakes out.

What provider stress looks like from the customer side

For buyers, provider financial stress shows up before any announcement does, and the symptoms are specific. Capacity rationing. Lower responsiveness for non-enterprise customers. Sudden pricing changes. Those are what a provider does when utilization is below break-even and cash is tight, and they are visible to a customer well before a shutdown notice.

There is a pricing tell worth understanding too. Providers financed through vendor arrangements carry locked-in cost structures tied to revenue-share terms, so their on-demand pricing has to cover both debt service and the vendor's cut. Providers without vendor-financed capital expenditure can price closer to market because they are not servicing those obligations. A price that seems inexplicably high may be structural rather than opportunistic.

The consequences of a mid-contract exit are worse than an inconvenience. Workload migration under time pressure, service disruption, renegotiated pricing from a weak position, and in the worst case stranded workloads with no clear recovery path.

...

Why did GPU providers fail in the first half of 2026?+

Three pressures converged: capital raised in a different rate environment coming due, expanded Blackwell supply shifting advantage toward volume buyers, and hyperscaler price cuts narrowing the differentiation. H100 spot pricing at $1.99 an hour sat below the cost basis for debt-financed providers, which made the revenue side unworkable regardless of operational quality.

...

Analysis across multiple sources puts it at five to seven surviving the next 18 to 24 months as standalone businesses, from well over a hundred competing today. Others will be acquired rather than shut down, which is a different outcome for their customers but still a contract renegotiation.
